'''''Conium maculatum''''', commonly known as '''hemlock''' ([[British English]]) or '''poison hemlock''' (in North America), is a highly poisonous [[flowering plant]]  and a [[Nitrophily|nitrophile]] weed species in the carrot family [[Apiaceae]].

The plant is [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]], with no woody parts, and has a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] lifecycle. Under the right conditions, the plant grows quite rapidly during the growing season and can reach heights of {{Convert|8|ft|abbr=off|order=flip}} with a long [[Taproot|penetrating root]]. The plant has a distinctive odour that is usually considered unpleasant and carries with the wind. The hollow stems are usually spotted dark maroon and turn dry and brown after the plant completes its biennial lifecycle.

Native to [[Europe]] and [[North Africa]], hemlock is a hardy plant that can live in a variety of environments. It is widely naturalised outside its native range, including in Australia, [[West Asia]], and North and [[South America]], where it can become an [[Invasive plant|invasive]] [[weed]].<!--lead just summarizes cited text; please don't add anything 'new' up here-->

All parts of the plant are [[Toxic plant|toxic]], particularly the seeds and roots, and especially when ingested. Hemlock is well-known as the poison that killed the philosopher [[Socrates]] after [[Trial of Socrates|his trial]] in [[Ancient Greece]].

== Description ==

''Conium maculatum'' is a herbaceous [[flowering plant]] that typically grows as a [[biennial plant|biennial]], but can grow as a [[perennial]] on occasion.<ref name="Pokorny-2018">{{Cite web |last1=Pokorny |first1=Monica |last2=Davis |first2=Stacy |last3=Mangold |first3=Jane |date=January 2018 |title=Poison Hemlock ''Conium maculatum'' |url=http://store.msuextension.org/publications/AgandNaturalResources/MT200013AG.pdf |website=Montana State University Extension |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240730204857/http://store.msuextension.org/publications/AgandNaturalResources/MT200013AG.pdf |archive-date=30 July 2024 |access-date=22 August 2025}}</ref> It is a nitrophile.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Vetter |first=J. |date=2004-09-01 |title=Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum L.) |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278691504001309 |journal=[[Food and Chemical Toxicology]] |volume=42 |issue=9 |pages=1373–1382 |doi=10.1016/j.fct.2004.04.009|pmid=15234067 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The second year stems topped with flowers grow to between {{cvt|0.5 and 3|m|ft}} in height;<ref name="Heil-2013">{{Cite book |last1=Heil |first1=Kenneth D. |last2=O'Kane |first2=Steve L. Jr. |last3=Reeves |first3=Linda Mary |last4=Clifford |first4=Arnold |date=2013 |title=Flora of the Four Corners Region: Vascular Plants of the San Juan River Drainage, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah |url=https://archive.org/details/mobot31753003888887 |edition=First |location=St. Louis, Missouri |publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] |page=114 |isbn=978-1-930723-84-9 |lccn=2012949654 |oclc=859541992}}</ref> they are coarse and branch frequently.<ref name="Welsh-1987">{{Cite book <!--Deny Citation Bot--> |last1=Welsh |first1=Stanley L. |author-link1=Stanley Larson Welsh |last2=Atwood |first2=N. Duane |last3=Goodrich |first3=Sherel |last4=Higgins |first4=Larry C. |date=1987 |title=A Utah Flora |url=https://archive.org/details/utahflora0000unse |url-access=registration |series=Great Basin Naturalist Memoirs, No. 9 |edition=First |location=Provo, Utah |publisher=[[Brigham Young University]] |pages=353–354 |jstor=23377658 |oclc=9986953694 |access-date=22 August 2025}}</ref> Stems are hollow except at the joints where the leaves are attached and are generally spotted or streaked with [[purple]].<ref name="Pokorny-2018" /><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Constance |first1=Lincoln |author-link1=Lincoln Constance |last2=Wetherwax |first2=Margriet |date=2012 |title=''Conium maculatum'', in Jepson Flora Project |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=20136 |website=Jepson eFlora |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241204005949/https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=20136 |archive-date=4 December 2024 |access-date=22 August 2025}}</ref> In the first year of growth, the plant has no stems and produces a large [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]] of leaves.<ref name="Pokorny-2018" /> All parts of the plant are [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]], lacking hairs, but sometimes they will have a small amount of blue-grey natural waxes on lower parts of the plant.<ref name="Moazzami-2020">{{cite book |last1=Moazzami Farida |first1=Seyed Hamed |last2=Ghorbani |first2=Abdolbaset |last3=Bussmann |first3=Rainer W. |author-link3=Rainer W. Bussmann |last4=Batsatsashvili |first4=Ketevan |last5=Kikvidze |first5=Zaal |date=2020 |chapter=''Conium maculatum'' L. Apiaceae |editor-last1=Batsatsashvili |editor-first1=Ketevan |editor-last2=Kikvidze |editor-first2=Zaal |editor-last3=Bussmann |editor-first3=Rainer W. |editor-link3=Rainer W. Bussmann |title=Ethnobotany of the Mountain Regions of Far Eastern Europe: Ural, Northern Caucasus, Turkey, and Iran |page=312 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-28940-9_148 |isbn=978-3-030-28940-9 |oclc=1156345046}}</ref> The [[taproot]] is long, white, has a fleshy texture, and is usually unbranched.<ref name="Cooper-1998">{{cite book |last1=Cooper |first1=Marion R. |last2=Johnson |first2=Anthony W. |title=Poisonous Plants and Fungi in Britain: Animal and Human Poisoning |date=1998 |publisher=[[Stationery Office (UK)|Stationery Office]] |location=London |isbn=978-0-11-242981-4 |oclc=39045741 |pages=220–222 |edition=Second}}</ref>

The [[leaves]] are one- to three-[[pinnate]], finely divided and lacy. The leaves lower down on the plant are two-pinnate or more, while the upper leaves are one-pinnate and often only partly divided. The lower leaves are larger than those higher up.<ref name="Heil-2013" /> They are broad with an overall triangular shape, some {{Cvt |30 to 60 |cm}} in length.<ref name="Moazzami-2020" /> The leaflets are attached in pairs on opposite sides of the central veins.<ref name="Welsh-1987" />

The poison hemlock's flowers are small and white; each flower has five petals and lacks [[sepal]]s.<ref name="Holm-1997">{{cite book |last1=Holm |first1=LeRoy G. |last2=Doll |first2=Jerry |last3=Holm |first3=Eric |last4=Herberger |first4=James |date=1997 |title=World Weeds: Natural Histories and Distribution |location=New York |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |pages=223, 225 |isbn=978-0-471-04701-8 |oclc=34114783}}</ref> The flowers have white [[stamen]]s and a [[Style (botany)|style]] that measures about 0.5 mm. The flowers are in umbrella shaped clusters called [[umbel]]s.<ref name="Heil-2013" /> They measure {{Cvt|2 to 5|cm|1}} in diameter and are found both at the end of stem branches and growing from the [[axil]]s, the angle created where the leaf stem joins the main stems of the plant. Each [[umbel]] is a circular cluster of ten to twenty rays, the short stems 1 to 3.5 cm long, radiating out from its center.<ref name="Clapham-1987">{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A. R. |author-link1=Arthur Roy Clapham |last2=Tutin |first2=T. G. |author-link2=Tom Tutin |last3=Moore |first3=D. M. |author-link3=David Moore (botanist born 1933) |date=1987 |title=Flora of the British Isles |url=https://archive.org/details/floraofbritishis0000clap |url-access=registration |edition=Third |location=Cambridge; New York |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |page=287 |isbn=978-0-521-30985-1 |oclc=13332738 |access-date=1 September 2025}}</ref>

The fruit is a [[schizocarp]],<ref name="Holm-1997" /> it can easily be separated into two parts.<ref name="Knight-2001">{{cite book |last1=Knight |first1=Anthony P. |last2=Walter |first2=Richard G. |date=2001 |title=A Guide to Plant Poisoning of Animals in North America |url=https://archive.org/details/guidetoplantpois0000knig |location=Jackson, Wyoming |publisher=Teton NewMedia |page=38 |isbn=978-1-893441-11-8 |oclc=43894438 |access-date=4 September 2025}}</ref> The fruits measure 2.5 to 3.5 mm long and are gray-brown with ridges and have an egg shaped outline.<ref name="Clapham-1987" /><ref name="Knight-2001" />

=== Similar species ===

[[File:Daucus carota Marchew zwyczajna 2023-07-23 Sołtysowice 02.jpg|thumb |upright |The wild carrot, ''[[Daucus carota]]'', is often confused with poison hemlock.]]

Hemlock can be confused with several other species in the parsley family with potentially fatal results. Edible plants that can be confused with hemlock include cultivated [[carrot]]s and the [[wild carrot]] (''Daucus carota''), [[parsnip]] (''Pastinaca sativa''), [[fennel]] (''Foeniculum vulgare''), and [[parsley]] (''Petroselinum crispum'').<ref name="Dauncey-2018">{{Cite book |last1=Dauncey |first1=Elizabeth A. |last2=Larsson |first2=Sonny |date=2018 |title=Plants That Kill: A Natural History of the World's Most Poisonous Plants |location=Princeton, New Jersey |publisher=Princeton University Press |pages=100−101 |isbn=978-0-691-17876-9 |oclc=1027707097}}</ref>

[[Daucus carota|Wild carrot]] has a hairy stem without purple markings, and grows less than {{Convert |1 |m |ft |abbr=on |frac=2}} tall.<ref name="Noxious Weeds-2016">{{cite web |date=November 28, 2016 |title=Poison-hemlock |url=http://www.kingcounty.gov/environment/animalsAndPlants/noxious-weeds/weed-identification/poison-hemlock.aspx |access-date=January 23, 2017 |work=Noxious Weeds in King County, Weed Identification Photos |location=Seattle, Washington |publisher=Department of Natural Resources and Parks, Water and Land Resources Division, Rural and Regional Services section }}</ref> One can distinguish the two from each other by hemlock's smooth texture, vivid mid-green colour, purple spotting of stems and petioles, and flowering stems reaching a typical height of at least {{Convert |1.5 |m |ft |abbr=on |frac=2}}—twice the maximum for wild carrot.<ref>{{cite book |last=Nyerges |first=Christopher |title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods |publisher=[[Falcon Guides]] |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3 |location=Guilford, Connecticut |oclc=965922681}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://ravensroots.org/blog/2015/6/26/poison-hemlock-id |title=How to Tell the Difference Between Poison Hemlock and Queen Anne's Lace |date=2 July 2015 |access-date=2021-05-03 |archive-date=2021-05-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210519074353/http://ravensroots.org/blog/2015/6/26/poison-hemlock-id |url-status=live }}</ref>

Hemlock can be confused with harmless cow parsley (''[[Anthriscus sylvestris]]''),<ref name="Pokorny-2018" /><ref name="USDA ARS">{{cite web |title=Poison Hemlock (Conium maculatum) |url=https://www.ars.usda.gov/pacific-west-area/logan-ut/poisonous-plant-research/docs/poison-hemlock-conium-maculatum/ |website=[[USDA Agricultural Research Service]] |access-date=26 October 2025}}</ref> the wild herb ''[[Chaerophyllum macropodum]]'' used in Turkish cheesemaking,<ref name="Frohne-2005" /> and deadly water hemlock (''[[Cicuta]]'').<ref name="USDA ARS"/> Water hemlock lacks the purple spots and the disagreeable mouse like smell of hemlock and has a branching [[tuber]] that grows sideways in the soil instead of a vertical [[taproot]].<ref name="Barceloux-2008">{{cite book |last1=Barceloux |first1=Donald G. |date=2008 |title=Medical Toxicology of Natural Substances: foods, fungi, medicinal herbs, plants, and venomous animals |location=Hoboken, New Jersey |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |page=796 |doi=10.1002/9780470330319.ch131 |isbn=978-0-471-72761-3 |oclc=299026676}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==

The generic name ''Conium'' comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] κώνειον ''kṓneion'': "hemlock". This may be related to ''konas'' (meaning to whirl), in reference to [[vertigo]], one of the symptoms of ingesting the plant.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Conium maculatum'' |url=http://jan.ucc.nau.edu/plants-c/bio414/species%20pages/conium%20maculatum.htm |access-date=2012-07-06 |publisher=Northwestern Arizona University |archive-date=2012-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120623113546/http://jan.ucc.nau.edu/plants-c/bio414/species%20pages/conium%20maculatum.htm }}</ref>

''C. maculatum'' was the first species within the genus ''[[Conium]]'' to be described. It was identified by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his 1753 publication, ''[[Species Plantarum]]''.<ref name="Parker-2015">{{Cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=Chris |title=Conium maculatum (poison hemlock) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/14820 |access-date=2020-12-03 |website=www.cabi.org |date=2015 |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=14820 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.14820 |doi-access=free }}</ref> ''Maculatum'' means 'spotted', in reference to the purple blotches on the plant's stalks and is derived from the Latin {{lang|la|macula}}.<ref>{{cite book |last=Casselman |first=Bill |author-link=Bill Casselman (writer) |date=1997 |title=Canadian Garden Words |url=https://archive.org/details/canadiangardenwo0000cass_e9c9 |url-access=registration |language=en |edition=First |location=Toronto, Canada |publisher=Little, Brown and Company |page=251 |isbn=978-0-316-13343-2 |oclc=37489809 |access-date=23 September 2025}}</ref>

''Conium maculatum'' has {{table row counter |id=Synonyms}} [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]], 16 of them species, according to [[Plants of the World Online]].<ref name="POWO-2025">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2025 |id=840668-1 |title=''Conium maculatum'' L. |access-date=26 August 2025}}</ref>

=== Names ===

In [[British English|British]], [[Australian English|Australian]], and [[New Zealand English]], the most prominent [[vernacular name]] is hemlock.<ref name="Atlas2020"/><ref name="Atlas of Living Australia" /><ref name="Holm-1997" /> This name is derived from the [[Old English]] words {{lang|ang|hymlice}}, {{lang|ang|hymlic}}, or {{lang|ang|hemlic}}, likely referring to ''Conium''. More certainly in the 1500s, it referred to ''Conium maculatum'' and was used in herbalist texts. It entered [[Middle English]] as {{lang|enm|hemeluc}}, {{lang|enm|hemlok}}, {{lang|enm|hemlake}}, {{lang|enm|hemlocke}}, {{lang|enm|hemloc}}, or {{lang|enm|hemblock}}. In this period, it was first spelled as ''hemlock'' by William Shakespeare in his play ''[[Henry V (play)|Henry V]]'' in 1623.<ref name="OUP">{{Cite OED|Hemlock, N. |2146562938}}</ref> The herbaceous plant is unrelated to [[conifer]]ous trees in the genus ''[[Tsuga]],'' which are also called hemlocks and were thought to have a similar smell.<ref name="Mitchell-1972">{{cite web |last=Mitchell |first=Alan |title=Conifers in the British Isles: a descriptive handbook |date=1972 | url=https://cdn.forestresearch.gov.uk/1972/03/fcbk033.pdf |page=302 |access-date=2024-10-24}}</ref>

In [[American English|American]] and [[Canadian English]],<ref name="NRCS-2024">{{cite usda plants |symbol=COMA2 |title=Conium maculatum L. |date=30 January 2024}}</ref><ref name="UBC-2025">{{cite web |last1=Acadia University |last2=Université de Montréal Biodiversity Centre |last3=University of Toronto Mississauga |last4=University of British Columbia |date=2025 |title=''Conium maculatum'' poison hemlock, though this name is also used elsewhere.<ref name="Atlas of Living Australia" /> This usage dates to 1757.<ref>{{Cite OED|Poison Hemlock, N. |5209466060}}</ref> Less frequent names used in both America and Australia include spotted hemlock and poison parsley.<ref name="Coffey-1993">{{cite book |last1=Coffey |first1=Timothy |date=1993 |title=The History and Folklore of North ==Distribution and habitat==

The hemlock plant is native to Europe, [[Central Asia]], and the [[Mediterranean region]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |date=18 August 2025 |title=''Conium maculatum'' in Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. Version 25.08 |url=http://www.worldplants.de?name=Conium-maculatum |website=World Plants |access-date=31 August 2025}}</ref> It occurs in many [[British Isles]] counties,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A. R. |author-link1=Arthur Roy Clapham |last2=Tutin |first2=T. G. |author-link2=Tom Tutin |last3=Warburg |first3=E. F. |author-link3=E. F. Warburg |date=1981 |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles |url=https://archive.org/details/excursionfloraof0000clap_t0h8 |url-access=registration |location=Cambridge; New York |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |page=195 |isbn=978-0-521-23290-6 |oclc=6249816 |access-date=30 August 2025}}</ref> including in [[Northern Ireland]].<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Hackney |editor-first=P. |date=1992 |title=Stewart & Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland |publisher=Institute of Irish Studies and [[Queen's University Belfast]] |isbn=0-85389-446-9}}</ref> It has become naturalised in Asia, North America, Australia, and New Zealand.<ref name="Schep-2009" /><ref name="Zehui-2017">{{cite web |last=Zehui |first=Pan |author2=Watson, Mark F. |title=31. ''Conium'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 243. 1753 |work=Flora of China |url= http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=107860 |access-date=January 23, 2017}} See also the substituent page: {{cite web |url= http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200015502 |access-date=January 23, 2017 |title=1. ''Conium maculatum'' Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 243. 1753 |work=Flora of China}}</ref><ref name="Atlas of Living Australia">{{Cite web |url=http://bie.ala.org.au/species/urn:lsid:biodiversity.org.au:apni.taxon:451627 |title=Atlas of Living Australia, ''Conium maculatum'' L., Carrot Fern |access-date=2015-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150919165822/http://bie.ala.org.au/species/urn:lsid:biodiversity.org.au:apni.taxon:451627 |archive-date=2015-09-19 }}</ref> It is sometimes encountered around rivers in [[Victoria (Australia)|southeast Australia]] and [[Tasmania]], where it has been considered an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Hemlock, Carrot Fern, Poison Hemlock, Poison Parsley, Spotted Hemlock, Wild Carrot, Wild Parsnip |url=https://weeds.org.au/profiles/hemlock-carrot-fern/ |website=Weeds Australia - profiles |publisher=Centre for Invasive Species Solutions |access-date=30 January 2024 |date=2021}}</ref> Infestations and human contact with the plant are sometimes newsworthy events in the U.S. due to its toxicity.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://beehabitat.com/poison-hemlock-can-kill-you-in-3-hours-or-less |title=Poison Hemlock |access-date=2022-11-29 |archive-date=2022-11-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221129033902/https://beehabitat.com/poison-hemlock-can-kill-you-in-3-hours-or-less/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.dallasnews.com/news/2023/06/03/poison-hemlock-was-spotted-in-a-dallas-suburb-heres-what-you-should-know-about-the-plant/ |first=Noor |last=Adatia |title=Poison hemlock was spotted in a Dallas suburb. Here's what you should know about the plant. |work=The Dallas Morning News |date=2023-06-03 |access-date=2023-06-03 |archive-date=2023-06-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230603204722/https://www.dallasnews.com/news/2023/06/03/poison-hemlock-was-spotted-in-a-dallas-suburb-heres-what-you-should-know-about-the-plant/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It spreads rapidly by seed, and is hard to eradicate as the seeds can lie dormant for up to 6 years.<ref name=toolate>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-17 |title=Poison Hemlock: TOO LATE! |url=https://bygl.osu.edu/node/1996 |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=bygl.osu.edu |language=en}}</ref>

==Ecology==

[[File:Agonopterix alstromeriana, Aberdovey, North Wales, July 2006 (20191381660).jpg|thumb |upright=0.6 |''[[Agonopterix alstroemeriana|Agonopterix alstromeriana]]'' moth; its larva feeds on hemlock plants.]]

The plant is often found in poorly drained soil, particularly near streams, ditches, and other watery surfaces. It grows on roadsides, at the edges of cultivated fields and in waste areas.<ref name="Schep-2009" /> It grows in quite damp soil,<ref name="Atlas2020">{{Cite web |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.brm |title=Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora: ''Conium maculatum'' |access-date=2014-08-07 |archive-date=2014-07-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714114749/http://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=plant%2Fconium-maculatum |url-status=live }}</ref> but also on drier rough grassland, roadsides, and [[disturbed ground]]. It is used as a food plant by the [[larva]]e of some [[Lepidoptera]], including [[silver-ground carpet]] moths and the poison hemlock moth (''[[Agonopterix alstroemeriana]]''). The latter has been widely used as a biological control agent for the plant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Castells |first1=Eva |last2=Berenbaum |first2=May R. |date=June 2006 |title=Laboratory Rearing of ''Agonopterix alstroemeriana'', the Defoliating Poison Hemlock (''Conium maculatum'' L.) Moth, and Effects of Piperidine Alkaloids on Preference and Performance |url=http://ddd.uab.cat/record/125702 |journal=[[Environmental Entomology]] |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=607–615 |doi=10.1603/0046-225x-35.3.607 |s2cid=45478867 |doi-access=free |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

It is a food source for caterpillars of the North American [[black swallowtail]] butterfly, though they have greater success on two other introduced plants, wild carrots and parsnips.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Feeny |first1=Paul |last2=Blau |first2=William S. |last3=Kareiva |first3=Peter M. |date=June 1985 |title=Larval Growth and Survivorship of the Black Swallowtail Butterfly in Central New York |journal=[[Ecological Monographs]] |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=167–187 |doi=10.2307/1942556 |jstor=1942556 |bibcode=1985EcoM...55..167F }}</ref> Similarly, the [[anise swallowtail]] (''Papilio zelicaon'') in western North America depends largely on non-native plants like hemlock and fennel in urban and suburban areas of [[California]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shapiro |first1=Arthur M. |date=January 2002 |title=The Californian urban butterfly fauna is dependent on alien plants |journal=Diversity and Distributions |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=34, 39 |doi=10.1046/j.1366-9516.2001.00120.x |jstor=3246685 |bibcode=2002DivDi...8...31S |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Poison hemlock was introduced to the US from Europe in the 1800s as an ornamental garden plant called "winter fern".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Exotic Species: Poison Hemlock (U.S. National Park Service) |url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/poison-hemlock.htm |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=www.nps.gov |language=en}}</ref> With it came the poison hemlock moth, which has spread across most of the US, but its efficacy at destroying the plant has been limited. The plant may be adapting to its predators by becoming more toxic.<ref name=toolate/>

==Toxicity==

All parts of the plant can be poisonous, but the total amount of poisonous [[alkaloid]]s varies significantly with the age of the plant and between parts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peddinti |first1=Gopal |last2=Hotti |first2=Hannu |last3=Teeri |first3=Teemu H. |last4=Rischer |first4=Heiko |date=20 October 2022 |title=De novo transcriptome assembly of ''Conium maculatum'' L. to identify candidate genes for coniine biosynthesis |journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |volume=12 |issue=1 |article-number=17562 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-21728-w |pmid=36266299 |doi-access=free|pmc=9584964 |bibcode=2022NatSR..1217562P }}</ref> The roots of young, first-year plants contain only traces of poison or none at all.<ref name="Cromwell-1956">{{cite journal |last1=Cromwell |first1=B. T. |date=1 October 1956 |title=The separation, micro-estimation and distribution of the alkaloids of hemlock (''Conium maculatum'' L.) |journal=[[Biochemical Journal]] |volume=64 |issue=2 |pages=259–266 |doi=10.1042/bj0640259 |pmid=13363836|pmc=1199726 }}</ref><ref name="Fairbairn-1961">{{cite journal |last1=Fairbairn |first1=J.W. |last2=Suwal |first2=P.N. |date=October 1961 |title=The alkaloids of hemlock (''Conium maculatum'' L.).—II |url=http://wxjs.chinayyhg.com/upload/Files/Phytochemistry/1961-1962-Vol.01/Vol.1(1961-1962)/Issue-1-pp1-62/38.pdf |journal=[[Phytochemistry (journal)|Phytochemistry]] |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=39–46 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)82809-5 |bibcode=1961PChem...1...39F |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603225935/http://wxjs.chinayyhg.com/upload/Files/Phytochemistry/1961-1962-Vol.01/Vol.1(1961-1962)/Issue-1-pp1-62/38.pdf |archive-date=3 June 2024 |access-date=3 September 2025}}</ref> The leaves of [[seedling]]s have lower levels of poison than slightly older plants. In the spring of the second year the leaves are highly toxic, though not as poisonous as the flowers or seeds later in the season.<ref name="Cromwell-1956" /> The hollow stems remain deadly for up to three years after the plant has died.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Duggan |first=Scott |date=1 June 2018 |title=Poison hemlock and Western waterhemlock: deadly plants that may be growing in your pasture |url=https://extension.oregonstate.edu/crop-production/pastures-forages/poison-hemlock-western-waterhemlock-deadly-plants-may-be-growing |journal=Ag - Forages/Pastures}}</ref> However, drying causes the plant to lose a large part of its toxic compounds.<ref name="Cooper-1998" /> Plants which grew in sunny conditions can be twice as poisonous as plants that grew in wet and cloudy conditions.<ref name="Cooper-1998" />

The main toxic [[alkaloid]]s are [[coniine]] and γ-coniceine,<ref name="Frohne-2005">{{cite book |last1=Frohne |first1=Dietrich |last2=Pfänder |first2=Hans Jürgen |date=2005 |orig-date=Translated from German Fifth Edition 2004 |editor-last1=McKinney |editor-first1=Patrick |editor-last2=Cumpston |editor-first2=Kirk |title=Poisonous Plants: A Handbook for Doctors, Pharmacists, Toxicologists, Biologists and Veterinarians |translator-last1=Alford |translator-first1=Inge |edition=Second |location=Portland, Oregon |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |pages=47–49 |isbn=978-0-88192-750-4 |oclc=59360317}}</ref> also called gamma-coniceine.<ref name="Green-2024">{{cite web |last1=Green |first1=J. D. |last2=Romano |first2=Megan |last3=Arnold |first3=Michelle |title=Act Now to Control Poison Hemlock |url=https://u.osu.edu/beef/2024/03/13/act-now-to-control-poison-hemlock/ |publisher=[[Ohio State University]] |access-date=3 September 2025 |date=13 March 2024}}</ref> Intoxication is reported in diverse groups of animals including pigs, bovids, turkeys, equines, rabbits,<ref name="Frohne-2005"/><ref name="Hotti-2017"/> cats, and dogs.<ref name="USDA ARS"/> However, [[songbird]]s are less sensitive and have reportedly become toxic from absorbing the coniine from hemlock.<ref name="Frohne-2005" /> Ingesting more than 150–300 milligrams of coniine, approximately equivalent to six to eight hemlock leaves, can be fatal for adult humans.<ref name="Hotti-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Hotti |first1=Hannu |last2=Rischer |first2=Heiko |title=The killer of Socrates: Coniine and Related Alkaloids in the Plant Kingdom |journal=Molecules |date=14 November 2017 |volume=22 |issue=11 |page=1962 |pmid=29135964 |pmc=6150177 |doi-access=free |doi=10.3390/molecules22111962}}</ref>

Grazing animals are most likely to be poisoned in the spring when other [[forage]] is unavailable.<ref name="Frohne-2005" /> However, they may also be poisoned when hemlock has become mixed into grain, [[hay]], or [[silage]].<ref name="Green-2024" /> Poison hemlock ingestion typically induces intense and fatal seizures in cattle. Even very small quantities have been shown to cause birth defects when ingested within 40–100 days of gestation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Haying and Cattle Grazing Areas with Hemlock {{!}} UNL Beef {{!}} Nebraska |url=https://beef.unl.edu/beefwatch/2024/haying-and-cattle-grazing-areas-hemlock/ |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=beef.unl.edu}}</ref>

Hemlock was one of many plants suggested by medieval writers as a possible cause of [[coturnism]], a disease caused by eating [[common quail]] in certain seasons. Modern research focuses on [[annual woundwort]] (''Stachys annua'') as the most likely source of the toxin, though the cause is still unknown.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bartram |first1=Stefan |last2=Boland |first2=Wilhelm |date=5 November 2001 |title=Chemistry and Ecology of Toxic Birds |journal=[[ChemBioChem]] |volume=2 |issue=11 |pages=809–811 |doi=10.1002/1439-7633(20011105)2:11<809::AID-CBIC809>3.0.CO;2-C |pmid=11948866 }}</ref>

===Alkaloids===

[[File:(S)-Coniine Structural Formula V.1.svg|thumb |(S)-(+)-coniine is the prevalent [[enantiomer]] found in ''Conium maculatum''.<ref name="Lee-2008">{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Stephen T. |last2=Green |first2=Benedict T. |last3=Welch |first3=Kevin D. |last4=Pfister |first4=James A. |last5=Panter |first5=Kip E. |year=2008 |title=Stereoselective potencies and relative toxicities of coniine enantiomers |journal=[[Chemical Research in Toxicology]] |volume=21 |issue=10 |pages=2061–2064 |doi=10.1021/tx800229w |pmid=18763813 }}</ref>]]

''Conium'' contains the [[piperidine alkaloids]] [[coniine]], [[N-methylconiine]], [[conhydrine]], {{chem name |pseudoconhydrine}}, and gamma-coniceine (or g-coniceïne), which is the precursor of the other hemlock alkaloids.<ref name="Schep-2009">{{cite journal |last1=Schep |first1=L. J. |last2=Slaughter |first2=R. J. |last3=Beasley |first3=D. M. |title= Nicotinic Plant Poisoning |journal=[[Clinical Toxicology]] |volume=47 |issue=8 |pages=771–781 |year=2009 |pmid=19778187 |doi=10.1080/15563650903252186 |s2cid=28312730}}</ref><ref name="Reynolds-2005">{{cite journal |last=Reynolds |first=T. |title=Hemlock Alkaloids from Socrates to Poison Aloes |journal=[[Phytochemistry (journal)|Phytochemistry]] |volume=66 |issue=12 |pages=1399–1406 |date=June 2005 |pmid=15955542 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2005.04.039 |bibcode=2005PChem..66.1399R }}</ref><ref name="Vetter-2004">{{cite journal |last1=Vetter |first1=J. |date=September 2004 |title=Poison hemlock (''Conium maculatum'' L.) |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8474788 |journal=[[Food and Chemical Toxicology]] |volume=42 |issue=9 |pages=1373–1382 |doi=10.1016/j.fct.2004.04.009 |pmid=15234067}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.toxinz.com/Demo/6/UExIMDIyLzEwNGg= |title=''Conium maculatum'' TOXINZ - Poisons Information |website=www.toxinz.com |access-date=2017-05-29 |archive-date=2017-05-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170523120448/http://www.toxinz.com/Demo/6/UExIMDIyLzEwNGg= }}</ref>

The major alkaloid found in flower buds is γ-coniceine. This molecule is transformed into coniine during the later stages of fruit development.<ref name="Cromwell-1956"/> The alkaloids are volatile; as such, researchers assume that these alkaloids play an important role in attracting [[pollinator]]s, such as butterflies and bees.<ref>{{cite book |last=Roberts |first=Margaret F. |chapter=Enzymology of Alkaloid Biosynthesis |date=1998 |pages=109–146 |publisher=Springer US |isbn=978-1-4419-3263-1 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-2905-4_5 |title=Alkaloids}}</ref>

=== Toxicology ===

Coniine has [[Pharmacology|pharmacological]] properties and a chemical structure similar to [[nicotine]].<ref name="Schep-2009"/><ref name="Brooks-2010">{{cite web |last=Brooks |first=D. E. |title=Plant Poisoning, Hemlock |date=2010-06-28 |url=http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/821362-overview |publisher=[[eMedicine]] |work=MedScape |access-date=2012-03-02}}</ref> Coniine acts directly on the [[central nervous system]] through inhibitory action on [[nicotinic acetylcholine receptors]]. Coniine can be dangerous to humans and [[livestock]],<ref name="Vetter-2004" /> and with its high potency, the ingestion of seemingly small doses can easily result in respiratory collapse and death.<ref>{{cite book |title=Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West |last=Tilford |first=Gregory L. |isbn=978-0-87842-359-0 |year=1997 |publisher=[[Mountain Press Publishing Company|Mountain Press]] }}</ref>

In laboratory experiments on mice, γ-coniceine was lethal at just 0.14 the equivalent dose of coniine while [[N-Methylconiine|N-methylconiine]] took 1.5 times the equivalent dose of coniine when injected. Oral administration of coniine required about five times as much for a lethal dose. Compared to coniine by oral administration γ-coniceine required 0.12 times as much and N-methylconiine required 2.0 times as much.<ref name="Bowman-1963" />

The alkaloid content in ''C. maculatum'' affects the [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulatory]] centre by a phenomenon called [[peripheral vasoconstriction]], resulting in [[hypothermia]] in calves.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=López |first1=T.A. |last2=Cid |first2=M.S. |last3=Bianchini |first3=M.L. |date=June 1999 |title=Biochemistry of hemlock (''Conium maculatum'' L.) alkaloids and their acute and chronic toxicity in livestock. A review |journal=[[Toxicon]] |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=841–865 |doi=10.1016/s0041-0101(98)00204-9 |pmid=10340826 |bibcode=1999Txcn...37..841L}}</ref> In addition, the alkaloid content stimulates the [[sympathetic ganglia]] and reduces the influence of the [[parasympathetic ganglia]] in rats and rabbits, causing an increased heart rate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Forsyth |first1=Carol S. |last2=Frank |first2=Anthony A. |date=July 1993 |title=Evaluation of developmental toxicity of coniine to rats and rabbits |journal=Teratology |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=59–64 |doi=10.1002/tera.1420480110 |pmid=8351649}}</ref>

Coniine has significant toxic effects on the kidneys. The presence of [[rhabdomyolysis]] and [[acute tubular necrosis]] has been demonstrated in patients who died from hemlock poisoning. Some of these patients had [[acute kidney injury]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Clinical spectrum of accidental hemlock poisoning: neurotoxic manifestations, rhabdomyolysis and acute tubular necrosis |pmid=1798593 |volume=6 |issue=12 |year=1991 |journal= Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation|pages=939–943 |last1=Rizzi |first1=D. |last2=Basile |first2=C |last3=Di Maggio |first3=A. |display-authors=et al |doi=10.1093/ndt/6.12.939}}</ref>
Contact of the leaves with bare skin can result in rash and persistent blisters through [[phototoxicity]], the sensitisation of the skin to sunlight.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mulligan |first1=Gerald A. |last2=Munro |first2=Derek B. |date=1990 |title=Poisonous Plants of Canada |url=https://archive.org/details/poisonousplantso00mull |url-access=registration |location=Ottawa, Canada |publisher=Agriculture Canada |page=48 |isbn=978-0-660-13467-3 |oclc=27770845 |access-date=23 September 2025}}</ref>

Shortly after ingestion, the alkaloids induce neuromuscular dysfunction that is potentially fatal due to failure of the [[respiratory system|respiratory muscle]]s. [[Acute toxicity]], if not lethal, may be followed by spontaneous recovery, provided further exposure is avoided. Death can be prevented by [[mechanical ventilation|artificial ventilation]] until the effects wear off after 48–72 hours.<ref name="Schep-2009" /> For an adult, the ingestion of more than 100 mg (0.1 gram) of coniine (about six to eight fresh leaves, or a smaller dose of the seeds or root) may be fatal. [[Unconsciousness|Narcosis]]-like effects can be observed as soon as 30 minutes after ingestion of green leaves of the plant, with victims falling asleep and gradually becoming unconscious until death occurs a few hours later.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Drummer |first1=Olaf H. |first2=Anthony N. |first3=Paul J. |first4=Kerryn L. |first5=Michael H. |last2=Roberts |last3=Bedford |last4=Crump |last5=Phelan  |title=Three deaths from hemlock poisoning |pmid=7791646 |volume=162 |issue=5 |year=1995 |pages=592–593 |journal=[[Medical Journal of Australia]] |doi=10.5694/j.1326-5377.1995.tb138553.x |s2cid=45736238 }}</ref> The onset of symptoms is similar to that caused by [[curare]], with an ascending muscular paralysis leading to paralysis of the respiratory muscles and ultimately death by oxygen deprivation.<ref>{{cite book |last=Higa de Landoni |first=Julia |title=Conium maculatum L. (Poisons Information Monograph 144) |date=1990 |publisher=[[International Programme on Chemical Safety]] (IPCS) |url=https://www.inchem.org/documents/pims/plant/conium.htm}}</ref>

The English physician and botanist [[John Harley (physician)|John Harley]] worked with a preparation of hemlock called ''succus conii'', testing it on himself and recording the effects in his book ''The Old Vegetable Neurotics'' published in 1869.<ref name="Bloch-2002">{{Cite book |last1=Bloch |first1=Enid |date=2002 |chapter=Hemlock Poisoning and the Death of Socrates: Did Plato Tell the Truth? |editor-last1=Brickhouse |editor-first1=Thomas C. |editor-last2=Smith |editor-first2=Nicholas D. |title=The Trial and Execution of Socrates: Sources and Controversies |location=New York |publisher=Oxford University Press |pages=256–259, 261–264, 272 |isbn=978-0-19-511980-0 |oclc=47677838}}</ref>

<blockquote> An hour and a quarter after taking the dose, I first felt decided weakness in my legs. The giddiness and diminution of motor power continued to increase for the next fifteen minutes. An hour and a half after taking the dose, these effects attained their maximum; and at this time I was cold, pale, and tottering. ...  The mind remained perfectly clear and calm, and the brain active throughout; but the body seemed heavy, and well-nigh asleep.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Harley |first1=John |author-link1=John Harley (physician) |date=1869 |title=The Old vegetable Neurotics: Hemlock, Opium, Belladonna and Henbane; Their Physiological Action and Therapeutical Use, Alone and in Combination; Being the Gulstonian Lectures of 1868, Extended and Including a Complete Examination of the Active Constituents of Opium |url=https://archive.org/details/oldvegetableneur00harl |location=London |publisher=Macmillan and Co. |pages=4–5 |oclc=963795665 |access-date=5 September 2025}}</ref></blockquote>

As there is no specific antidote, prevention is the only way to deal with agricultural production losses caused by the plant. The use of [[herbicide]]s and grazing with less-susceptible animals (such as sheep) have been suggested as control methods. Contrary to popular belief, scientific studies have disproven the claim that the plant's alkaloids can enter the human food chain via [[milk]] and [[fowl]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Frank |first1=A. A. |last2=Reed |first2=W. M. |date=April 1990 |title=Comparative Toxicity of Coniine, an Alkaloid of ''Conium maculatum'' (Poison Hemlock), in Chickens, Quails, and Turkeys |journal=[[Avian Diseases]] |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=433–437 |doi=10.2307/1591432 |jstor=1591432 |pmid=2369382 }}</ref>

== In culture ==

=== Ancient Greece ===

{{anchor |Socrates}}<!-- This Anchor tag serves to provide a permanent target for incoming section links. Please do not remove it, nor modify it, except to add another appropriate anchor. -->
In ancient Greece, hemlock was used to poison condemned prisoners. ''Conium maculatum'' is the plant that killed [[Theramenes]], [[Socrates]], [[Polemarchus]], and [[Phocion]].<ref name="Blamey-2003">{{cite book |last1=Blamey |first1=Marjorie  |author1-link=Marjorie Blamey |last2=Fitter |first2=Richard |author2-link=Richard Fitter |last3=Fitter |first3=Alistair  |author3-link=Alistair Fitter |year=2003 |title=Wild flowers of Britain and Ireland: The Complete Guide to the British and Irish Flora |publisher=[[A & C Black]] |location=London |isbn=978-1-4081-7950-5}}</ref> Socrates, the most famous victim of hemlock poisoning, was sentenced to death at [[Trial of Socrates|his trial]]; he took an [[infusion]] of hemlock.<ref>{{cite book |last=Nails |first=Debra |author-link=Debra Nails |chapter=The Trial and Death of Socrates |editor-last1=Ahbel-Rappe |editor-first1=Sara |editor-last2=Kamtekar |editor-first2=Rachana |title=A Companion to Socrates |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WwpZVuylPgYC |year=2009 |publisher=[[Wiley (publisher)|Wiley]] |isbn=978-1-4051-5458-1 |pages=5–20}}</ref> In [[Greek mythology]], poisonous plants like hemlock were sacred to the goddess [[Hecate]] and her daughters [[Circe]] and [[Medea]].<ref name="Keezer-1963">{{cite journal |last=Keezer |first=William S. |title=Botanical Sources of Early Medicines |journal=[[BIOS (journal)|Bios]] |date=1963 |volume=34 |issue=4 |pages=185–191 |jstor=4606514}}</ref>

=== Uses ===

In high mountain areas of [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], hemlock leaves were used as a spring food after long winters. It required careful cooking, often in several changes of water. Other poisonous leaves used in this fashion included [[cow parsnip]]s (''Heracleum'' species), [[potato]]es, and [[lilies]]. Locals speaking to [[ethnobotanical]] researchers knew the poisonous nature of the plants and reported the practice to have largely died out with better roads and greater availability of cultivated foods in markets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bussmann |first1=Rainer W. |last2=Paniagua Zambrana |first2=Narel Y. |last3=Sikharulidze |first3=Shalva |last4=Kikvidze |first4=Zaal |last5=Kikodze |first5=David |last6=Tchelidze |first6=David |last7=Khutsishvili |first7=Manana |last8=Batsatsashvili |first8=Ketevan |last9=Hart |first9=Robbie E. |display-authors=5 |date=December 2016 |title=A comparative ethnobotany of Khevsureti, Samtskhe-Javakheti, Tusheti, Svaneti, and Racha-Lechkhumi, Republic of Georgia (Sakartvelo), Caucasus |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=11 |doi=10.1186/s13002-016-0110-2 |pmid=27659258 |doi-access=free|pmc=5034577 }}</ref>

Hemlock was used as a medicine in ancient times, though great care was required due to its toxicity. In [[Medieval Europe]], it was only administered as a remedy for [[rabies]], known at the time as "the bite of mad dogge", taken in wine together with [[Stachys|betony]] and [[fennel]] seed.<ref name="Mitich 1998">{{cite journal |last=Mitich |first=Larry W. |title=Intriguing World of Weeds: Poison-Hemlock (Conium maculatum L.) |journal=[[Weed Technology]] |date=1998 |volume=12 |pages=194–197 |doi=10.1017/S0890037X00042792 |url=https://my.ucanr.edu/repository/fileaccess.cfm?article=167062&p=PLQCSV}}</ref> Later uses included a final, desperate attempt to cure virulent poisons such as strychnine. In the 1400s and 1500s European monks roasted the root and applied it externally to the feet, hands, and wrists for pain from [[gout]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Le Strange |first=Richard |date=1977 |title=A History of Herbal Plants |url=https://archive.org/details/historyofherbalp0000lest_x7u7 |url-access=registration |location=New York |publisher=Arco Publishing |page=89 |isbn=978-0-668-04247-5 |oclc=2837368 |access-date=30 August 2025}}</ref> The popular herbalist [[Nicholas Culpeper]] wrote in the 1650s that it was under the control of [[Saturn (astrology)|Saturn]] giving it a cold and dangerous character. He recommended it for external use for inflammation and swelling and the roasted root on the hands for gout.<ref name="Keezer-1963"/> From the 1760s, it was applied to cancerous ulcers.<ref name="Mitich 1998"/>

In the Victorian [[language of flowers]], hemlock flowers were used as a symbol meaning, "You will be the death of me".<ref name="Lawton-2007"/> From 1864 to 1898 hemlock was officially listed as a medicine in the [[Pharmacopoeia#London, Edinburgh, Dublin|London]] and [[Edinburgh Pharmacopoeia|Edinburgh pharmacopoeias]]. The last listing of it was in the British Pharmaceutical Codex in 1934.<ref name="Bowman-1963">{{cite journal |last1=Bowman |first1=W. C. |last2=Sanghvi |first2=I. S. |date=1 September 1963 |title=Pharmacological Actions of Hemlock (''Conium Maculatum'') Alkaloids |journal=[[Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology]] |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=1–25 |doi=10.1111/j.2042-7158.1963.tb12738.x |eissn=2042-7158 |pmid=14014656}}</ref>

== Removal ==
If the infestation is relatively small, it is recommended to dig out the entire plant including the roots with proper protective equipment. One should wear clothing that covers exposed skin, eye protection, and gloves. Many herbicides will also work for killing a spread of hemlock.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-06-21 |title=Use caution with poison hemlock, ivy and oak - Oklahoma State University |url=https://extension.okstate.edu/articles/2022/poison_hemlock.html |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=extension.okstate.edu |language=en}}</ref>
